extracted.intended_audience: general readers of early-18th-century periodical essays; readers interested in manners, arts, and morals
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis/extraction from The Spectator (Addison & Steele) periodical essays — moral, artistic, and social observations intended for a broad literate public. The texts give prescriptive remarks on conduct, taste, and judgement rather than formal evaluation rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female public conduct / virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Female Virtues are of a Domestick Turn. The Family is the proper Province for Private Women to shine in. Women should distinguish themselves as tender Mothers and faithful Wives rather than as furious Partizans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice and examples: English women (being the most beautiful) should excel in accomplishments proper to their sex and avoid engaging in political competitions and contentions (the Greeks forbade women at the Olympic Games). If women display public spirit, it should be directed against obvious enemies of faith, liberty and country (example: Roman ladies contributing rings and jewels in time of public exigence, which thereafter allowed them public orations at funerals). Anti-patterns: women acting as 'furious Partizans' or engaging in factional hostilities with countrymen or co-religionists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal finance prudence / avoiding debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Running into debt reveals a baseness of spirit: 'The same little Mind was insolent in Riches, and shameless in Poverty.' A man in debt compromises his honour, liberty, and fortune; debt places him in a servile condition toward many people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel and examples: live within means, avoid ostentation and maintaining a false retinue or grandeur that leads to generational indebtedness (father mortgages, son inherits encumbrances). Case studies: Sir Andrew (laudable for never being sued) contrasted with Jack Truepenny (gullible surety, squandered estate). Anti-patterns: credulous generosity, acting as surety for others, using luxury to keep appearances. Moral/legal note: creditor may (legally) seize person or reputation; debt is socially and legally perilous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of good painting and types of artistic fault
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful taxonomy of artist-types and the virtues/vices of painting: VANITY (smiling, smirking faces, flashy drapery), STUPIDITY (mechanical copyist of vanity), FANTASQUE (distortions and grotesque chimeras), AVARICE (hasty, unfinished work), INDUSTRY (laborious, highly finished detail), ENVY (retoucher who aggravates defects), and TIME (the slow hand that mellows and perfects pictures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative guidance embedded in the allegory: value industry (careful, exhaustive workmanship — 'not omit a single Hair'), beware haste (AVARICE — unfinished works lose lasting beauty), beware vanity and over-decoration (gaudy colours and affected airs), and beware envious retouching that 'poisoned every Colour it touched.' Also: appreciate the positive effect of time — gradual wearing off of disagreeable gloss, added brown and mellowness that make a picture appear more perfect. Examples/anti-patterns: explicit descriptions of each bad type (Vanity's 'Petits Maitres', Fantasque's 'agreeable Monsters', Avarice's untidy dispatch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simplicity and naturalness in popular poetry/ballads
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain, simple copies of nature (e.g., the old ballad 'Two Children in the Wood') please because they present genuine, unaffected sentiments and incidents that grow naturally from the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic preference and defense: even when language is 'mean' or expression poor, genuine sentiment and natural incident excite pity and move readers. The critic should admire 'Nature in her Simplicity and Nakedness'; refined artifice is not always necessary. Anti-patterns: the 'little conceited Wits' who ridicule simple productions and fail to appreciate their natural force. Examples: comparisons to Virgil and note that great writers (Lord Dorset, Dryden) collected and enjoyed such ballads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy as a basis for judging character
rubrics_metrics.description: Every one is in some degree a master of physiognomy: 'Every Passion gives a particular Cast to the Countenance' and 'we may be better known by our Looks than by our Words.' The air of the whole face expresses inward disposition more than its lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical claim about human judgement: upon first encountering strangers, observers form immediate notions (proud, reserved, affable, good-natured) from looks; facial 'air' is more revealing than speech. Literary/theoretical support: Martial epigram and examples of faces likened to animals (ox, sheep, lion) to suggest temperament. Caveat/limit: the essayist leaves doctrinal questions (whether passions change facial mould or whether similar souls require similar habitations) to the curious, but asserts the practical efficacy of physiognomic judgement.
